title: Largest neuroimaging study of bulimia nervosa finds structural brain differences linked to diagnosis and binge-eating severity
content:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai found that individuals with bulimia nervosa have structural differences in brain regions involved in reward and motivation, as well as social and sensory processing, and that more frequent binge eating is associated with more widespread differences in brain structure, according to research published today in JAMA Psychiatry.
Bulimia nervosa is the second most common eating disorder in the world, characterized by recurrent binge eating and compensatory behaviors. Compared to other psychiatric illnesses, little is known about its neurobiology and previous neuroimaging studies have generally included small numbers of participants and produced inconsistent findings.
Laura A. Berner, PhD, Director of the Center for Computational Psychiatry at Mount Sinai, and colleagues from the global ENIGMA (Enhancing NeuroImaging Genetics through Meta-Analysis) consortium analyzed MRI brain scans from 369 females with bulimia nervosa and 417 females without an eating disorder across 17 international cohorts. In comparison to individuals without an eating disorder, those with bulimia nervosa had lower volume of the nucleus accumbens – a brain region involved in processing reward and motivation. They also had lower surface area in regions of the temporal cortex – a brain area involved in sensory and social processing. More frequent binge eating was associated with lower surface area in additional regions involved in cognitive control, reward value estimation, awareness of bodily signals, and processing and regulating emotions. In contrast, the frequency of compensatory behaviors - the measure currently used to define bulimia nervosa severity – was not associated with brain structure.
The findings suggest that specific symptoms, like binge eating, may have distinct neurobiological correlates. Because the study examined participants at a single point in time, longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these differences precede or follow illness onset.
This study gives us the clearest evidence to date that bulimia nervosa is associated with reproducible differences in brain structure. We were surprised that the differences we identified in the brain’s outer layer involved a structural feature that is largely established early in development.”
Laura A. Berner, PhD, Director of the Center for Computational Psychiatry, Mount Sinai
“Our findings raise important questions about whether some of these brain differences could be markers of vulnerability to developing the illness. At the same time, the findings should not be interpreted to mean that the brain is fixed, or that a person’s outcome is predetermined. We are excited about the next steps: understanding what these findings mean for the function of the affected brain circuits, and how these insights can ultimately help us identify better targets for prevention and treatment.”

title: Environmental Sustainability: Nigerian Breweries Plants 340,000 Trees, Restores Over 350 Hectares at Olokemeji Forest
content:
Latest Headlines
Environmental Sustainability: Nigerian Breweries Plants 340,000 Trees, Restores Over 350 Hectares at Olokemeji Forest
Dike Onwuamaeze
The Nigerian Breweries Plc (NB), in collaboration with the Ogun State Ministry of Forestry and International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has planted more than 340,000 indigenous trees and restored over 350 hectares of degraded forest landscape at the Olokemeji Forest within five years.
The Olokemeji Forest Reforestation Project, which is in line with NB’s “Brew a Better World” sustainability agenda, is aimed at advancing environmental stewardship and contributing to biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, watershed protection, and sustainable ecosystem management.
The milestone was highlighted during a joint engagement among the representatives of NB, the Ogun State Government and IITA, where stakeholders reviewed the project’s progress and reaffirmed their commitment to expanding collaborative efforts towards environmental restoration and sustainable land management.
Speaking during the engagement, the Director of Corporate Affairs, NB Plc, Mr. Uzodinma Odenigbo, disclosed that the initiative is part of ongoing efforts to strengthen ecosystem restoration and environmental sustainability in the communities where the company operates.
Odenigbo said: “At Nigerian Breweries, sustainability remains central to how we operate and create shared value.
“The restoration of over 350 hectares of degraded forest and the planting of more than 340,000 indigenous trees demonstrate what can be achieved through strategic partnerships.
“Beyond restoring ecosystems, we are investing in a healthier environment and creating opportunities that will benefit surrounding communities for generations to come.”
In his remarks, the Commissioner for Forestry, Ogun State, Mr. Oludotun Taiwo, commended the collaboration among the state government, NB Plc and IITA, noting that such partnerships are essential to preserving the state’s forest resources and promoting sustainable development.
Beyond reforestation, the Olokemeji Reforestation Project has also enhanced biodiversity, strengthened climate resilience, and improved watershed protection across the forest reserve.
The initiative has also created alternative livelihood opportunities for surrounding communities, including beekeeping and vegetable farming, and improving access to clean water by providing community boreholes.

title: Per-Aetiology Contrastive Severity Embeddings with Phonological Pseudo-Labelling for Multilingual Dysarthric Speech
content: Most multilingual dysarthria-severity systems either train on a single aetiology-language pair or pool heterogeneous aetiologies into one label space. We test that pooling assumption with four matched HuBERT-base contrastive embedding models under a shared backbone, training recipe, corpus registry and held-out evaluation: one mixed-aetiology baseline and three aetiology-specific models for cerebral palsy (CP), Parkinson's disease (PD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Training combines clinically labelled speech with ordinal pseudo-labels from a training-free phonological profiling method [1], [2]. On speaker-disjoint, leakage-filtered held-out subsets, the per-aetiology models outperform the mixed baseline across all three target aetiologies: CP (macro F1 0.829 vs 0.676, +22.6 % relative), PD (0.715 vs 0.511, +40.0 %) and ALS (0.788 vs 0.596, +32.3 %). On CP, adding 144 SAP and 44 CDSD pseudo-labelled speakers lifts macro F1 from 0.786 to 0.829 over a clinical-only CP model (+4.3 percentage points). Training data span three to seven languages per aetiology. We position this as a controlled comparison of label-space design choices and discuss pseudo-label calibration, split hygiene, and confidence-thresholded deployment as important limitations for future work.

title: B.C. judge rules Vancouver city candidates can use Chinese names on ballot
content:
B.C. judge rules Vancouver city candidates can use Chinese names on ballot
Judge Roger Cutler released his decision on Friday, but his written reason will come later
Seven Vancouver city candidates who included Chinese characters in their “usual” name can have them on the ballot for the municipal election, after the city lost a court challenge on Friday.
Judge Roger Cutler of the B.C. provincial court said each of the seven applicants would be allowed to use their usual names on the ballot for the Oct. 17 election and that he would issue his reasons for his decision at a later date.
Cutler said his decision should not be taken as a statement that the city’s application wasn’t appropriate, and his written reasons will provide guidance for future elections.
Lawyers for the city and for the candidates submitted arguments to Cutler on Wednesday and on Friday morning, and Cutler took five minutes after lunch to announce his decision.
The “usual names” in all seven cases included Chinese characters in addition to their “English” names, and the candidates argued the Vancouver Charter allowed that.
The city took the case to court, saying it wanted guidance on whether the Chinese character names were their “usual” names and whether they should be allowed on the ballots.
Cutler presided over the hearing by video from Duncan to eliminate any perception of bias from a Vancouver-based judge.
City lawyer Grant Murray told the court he would inform the chief election officer of the decision and that the decision had come in time for the lottery draw to determine the order of names on the ballots that was scheduled to be held at 5 p.m. Friday.
“I’m relieved by the decision,” Iona Bonamis, who’s running for city council under the OneCity party banner, said by phone.
She said hopefully it will mean candidates in future will be able to include the names they are known by in their community without having to go through a court battle.
A message left with the city for comment was not returned on Friday.
The city’s chief election officer, Jason Twa, had argued the seven Chinese character names were not part of their usual names.
In addition to Bonamis, whose name is 陶思穎 (To Sie Wing), the other candidates are current ABC councillor Lenny Zhou or 周楠 (Zhou Nan) and Christopher Lee, a OneCity school board candidate, whose Chinese name is pronounced Lee Kei Peng (李基鵬).
Others using Chinese character names are Yuk (Alfred) Chien (錢育廷), Yunzia (Chris) Qiu (仇云霞), Lorraine Lowe (刘黛明) and Shirley SiO (邵己凌). Lowe is running for city council, Qiu for park board and Chien and SiO for school board.
During his submissions, Murray had told court that all the candidates, with the exception of Bonamis, appeared to exclusively use their English names and not their Chinese names on social media.
And he said that it was “odd” that the candidates hadn’t included their “usual” Chinese names on their original filings but added them later, at the last minute.
Of the 123 candidates for council, park board and school board published on the City of Vancouver’s website, seven included a Chinese name.
The Charter is the unique provincial legislation that governs the City of Vancouver. According to the Charter, nomination papers must include the full name of the person nominated and “the usual name of the person nominated, if the full name of the person is different from the name the person usually uses.”
Bonamis said earlier if the court allowed her to use her name, it would send a message that Vancouver respects different cultures and that it’s a multicultural city.
Lee, 18, said it’s important for him to have the name on the ballot because “it’s a core part of my identity.”
“I’m a very proud Canadian. I’m also a very proud Chinese Canadian,” he said. “Canada is a multicultural place and we should respect that, the electoral office should respect that.”
“I don’t think it’s about having the Chinese name on the ballot to win votes, it’s about … our identity. It’s what the people in the Chinese community know us as.”
It’s a sign that we can “represent every single voice that Vancouver has,” he said.

title: Diesel refunds set to exit the VAT system
content:
Standalone refund system promises greater visibility, with both users and sellers required to register.
The South African Revenue Service (Sars) is introducing a new standalone diesel refund system that is being developed separately from the value-added tax (VAT) system. It forms part of Sars’s excise modernisation project.
All existing and new users will have to re-register on the new system, with the registration process starting on Monday (21 September).
In a significant change, both users and sellers of diesel will have to register, rather than only users. Claims for diesel purchased from a seller who is not registered with Sars will not qualify.
At a high level, there are certainly some positives to the new system, says Amanda Nkwanyana, a partner in the Webber Wentzel tax team.
“A standalone diesel refund system should, in principle, simplify administration and give both Sars and taxpayers greater visibility over registrations and claims. The move away from claiming through the VAT system may also create a more dedicated process for diesel refunds.”
Rules and rollout
Senior Sars officials on Friday shed light on the new system, the rules and the rollout process over the next couple of months.
The first phase is the registration of users and sellers.
Another change is the inclusion of contractors operating on a wet basis. Mahlatse Ledwaba, an excise specialist at Sars, says that under the current system only entities that purchase diesel for their own use qualify for the rebate.
Under the new system, contractors operating on behalf of other entities will also become eligible.
In terms of the new legislation, the qualifying categories are grouped into eight industries: agriculture (formerly farming and forestry), fishing, mining on land, offshore mining and offshore shipping, harbour shipping, rail freight transport, and electricity generation.
Registration applications can be submitted via eFiling or by booking an appointment at a branch office.
“Specific supporting documents, depending on the category, will be required and can be uploaded on the eFiling system.”
Ledwaba says applicants will receive an acknowledgement letter, a case number and a letter informing them of the outcome of their registration.
She stresses that until a “go-live date” has been announced, claims will continue to be submitted through the current system.
Deshen Pillay, a member of the team designing the electronic registration solution, says the registration process is split into three phases, with the registration of users and sellers as the starting phase.
The next phase will require users and sellers to declare their relationships to Sars. Nkwanyana says it appears that Sars intends to create a verified relationship between diesel sellers and users so that it can better monitor transactions and validate future claims.
Unanswered questions
“That being said, there are still a number of important practical questions that remain unanswered,” says Nkwanyana.
“Many taxpayers purchase diesel from multiple suppliers, but there was very little detail on how those multiple supplier relationships will be managed in practice, what administrative burden this may create, and what happens if one of those suppliers falls out of compliance.”
Another notable gap, she says, relates to logbooks and supporting records.
“Historically, the adequacy of logbooks and diesel usage records has been one of the biggest areas of dispute between Sars and taxpayers during diesel refund audits.”
She notes that the Sars webinar did not provide much detail on whether the substantiation requirements will change under the new system or how Sars intends to deal with these longstanding issues.
Ledwaba says there will be follow-up information sessions to inform taxpayers of all the requirements and assist them with the process as the system is rolled out.
The third phase will involve setting up users’ profiles. This will include their qualifying activities, site plans showing where the activities are performed, the equipment used, and the applicable licences and permits.
“This part is still under development and will only be implemented early next year. This will be in preparation for the second project, which is the actual claim functionality,” Pillay said during the webinar.
Key benefits
Chetan Vanmali, a leading indirect tax specialist at Webber Wentzel, identifies four key benefits:
- Improved transparency: Standalone administration should provide users with clearer visibility of registrations, claims, verifications and refund status.
- Better compliance and reduced fraud: Electronic registration, automated checks and seller-user relationship validation should strengthen compliance and reduce fraud.
- Faster processing: If Sars’s technology performs as intended, dedicated processing should allow diesel claims to be dealt with independently of Vat verifications and assessments.
- More predictable cash flow: Separating diesel refunds from Vat may reduce situations where diesel refund issues affect Vat refunds, or vice versa.
Since a large number of users and sellers must be registered and onboarded, the registration process has opened several months before the claim submission functionality becomes operational, Pillay says.
“This is to afford Sars sufficient time to onboard everyone and to be ready when the claim submission system is implemented,” he adds.
The new diesel refund system will only become effective once the claim submission functionality is implemented. Until then, claims will continue to be submitted through the existing Vat system.

title: Ekovinařství v Česku sílí, přírodě blízkých vinic přibývá. Odbyt však brzdí trend, že lidé přestávají pít alkohol
content:
Ekologickému vinařství se v Česku daří. Rozloha půdy, na které se víno pěstuje k přírodě šetrným způsobem, roste solidním tempem. Zatímco ještě v roce 2021 ekologické vinohrady zabíraly v celém Česku 876 hektarů, nyní, v roce 2026, je to již téměř 1300 hektarů a dalších dvě stě hektarů se na přechod do ekologického režimu chystá. To je dohromady pro představu rozloha dvou tisíc fotbalových hřišť. Ukazují to data Registru ekologických podnikatelů ministerstva zemědělství.
V Česku je nyní zhruba 17 tisíc hektarů vinic a ty ekologické tvoří necelých devět procent. „To je velmi dobré číslo,“ říká Kateřina Urbánková, manažerka PRO‑BIO – Svazu ekologických zemědělců. Podobný podíl totiž odpovídá i celosvětovému průměru rozlohy ekologických vinic.
Ekovinohradů začalo v Česku přibývat hlavně díky mnoha vinicím, které vstoupily do konverze, tedy přešly na ekologický režim, v letech 2022 a 2023, a mezitím dozrály do plné certifikace. „Ovšem nyní se přísun nových vinic, které postupně přecházejí do tohoto režimu, výrazně zpomalil, což může tempo růstu v příštích letech přibrzdit, pokud nezačnou přibývat noví zájemci,“ upozorňuje Urbánková.
Přípravek, který by se mohl používat napříč evropskou zemědělskou půdou
Co v současnosti nejvíce rozvoji ekologického vinařství v Česku pomáhá? Jednak dotační podpora, ale také technologie a poradenství. Zásadní pro vinaře je dostupnost funkčních prostředků ochrany rostlin pro ekologické vinohradnictví a s tím související odborné poradenství. Do budoucna by mohla pomoci i změna legislativy. „Pokud se podaří prosadit, aby byly přípravky na ochranu rostlin pro ekologické zemědělství schválené v některém státě EU automaticky použitelné v kterémkoliv státě, mohli by je využívat i čeští zemědělci. O tom se nyní jedná,“ říká Urbánková.
Podle Martina Chlada, prezidenta Svazu vinařů, rozvoj ekologických vinic pohání i tlak na ochranu krajiny a biodiverzity a potřeba reagovat na klimatickou změnu, stejně jako dostupnost nových odrůd odolných vůči houbovým chorobám. „Ekologické hospodaření je však náročnější na znalosti, organizaci práce i zvládání chorob a klimatických extrémů,“ konstatuje Chlad. I proto Svaz vinařů představil dlouhodobý strategický plán, jak obor rozvíjet v budoucích dvou dekádách. Navrhuje například, jak vinohradnictví adaptovat na změnu klimatu, jak v něm podporovat inovace, vzdělávání, vědu a výzkum nebo jak novelizovat legislativu.
Rozloha vinohradů dál klesla, je nejnižší od vstupu ČR do EU
Prodej ekologicky vyráběného vína v České republice roste, a to jak v absolutních číslech, tak jako podíl na celkovém trhu s vínem. Ovšem celková spotřeba vína v tuzemsku dlouhodobě klesá. „Mladí tolik nepijí, souvisí to se změnou pohledu na životosprávu. Díky teplému počasí mají vína více alkoholu, což nyní není příliš trend. Obecně prodej brzdí klesající spotřeba alkoholu, která tlačí na ekonomiku celého oboru,“ krčí rameny Urbánková. Dalšími bariérami jsou například omezené investiční možnosti, kdy návratnost investice do vinice je pro vinaře nejistá, stejně jako vyšší riziko výpadku úrody v mokrých letech a nižší výnosy oproti konvenčním vinohradům.
Ne jen módní trend, ale přesvědčení
Ekologické vinařství v Česku prošlo za třicet let od okrajové aktivity několika průkopníků k dynamicky rostoucímu segmentu, který dnes zahrnuje více než 160 registrovaných vinařů. První ekologické vinice se v tuzemsku objevily kolem roku 1990, zpočátku jen na velmi malých plochách a s omezeným počtem producentů.
K úplně prvním oficiálním výrobcům certifikovaného biovína v tuzemsku patří rodina Abrlova z Pavlova na Pálavě. Jak dnes Josef Abrle, syn zakladatele, říká, začínali s nadšením a bez dotací. „Bio, eko či jakkoliv to nazvete, takové zemědělství je jediné správné. Základem všeho je zdravá půda,“ říká. Dodává, že hnacím motorem podnikání v tomto oboru je pro něj víra, že po něm zůstane zdravá zem nepodléhající erozi a plná života. „Jen taková nás uživí,“ je přesvědčen Abrle.
I ostatní pionýrští ekovinaři svůj ekologický přístup k hospodaření na vinicích i výrobě ve sklepech nevnímají jako trendovou záležitost, ale spíše jako užitečnou práci pro životní prostředí. „Je to naše přesvědčení. Chceme udělat krajinu čistější pro naše potomky, zlepšit úrodnost a vitalitu půdy a vrátit do vinic živočichy a rostliny. A také pít čistá vína bez zbytečných éček,“ říká Adam Bednář, ředitel Rodinného vinařství Jedlička v Bořeticích na Břeclavsku. Jak sám říká, v ekorežimu fungují proto, že jej těší vidět vinice plné života, zelené a vitálnější. Sám však připouští, že s ekoprovozem se pojí více papírování a častější kontroly. „Ale to k tomu patří, když na ekologii bereme dotace,“ kvituje Bednář.
Ekovinař: Chceme víno bez pesticidů
Dalším výrazným producentem ekologických vín jsou Vinné sklepy Kutná Hora. Kromě vína vyrábějí i přírodní výluhy a přípravky na ekologické ošetřování vinic a jako jediní v Česku splňují certifikaci Demeter, což je nejpřísnější mezinárodní certifikace pro biodynamické zemědělství, která jde ještě nad rámec běžných standardů bioprodukce. Jak ředitel Lukáš Rudolfský říká, ekologické zemědělství respektuje přírodu a její zdroje. „Ale především to děláme pro sebe – chceme mít víno a další produkty zdravé, čisté, bez reziduí pesticidů,“ vysvětluje.
Baví ho také dobrý pocit, když se daří pěstovat révu v co největším souznění s okolní přírodou a s minimem ošetření, a když, tak většinou bylinkovými extrakty. Hnacím motorem jsou pro toto vinařství úspěchy na soutěžích v Česku i ve světě, stejně jako fakt, že ve vinařství probíhá dlouholetý výzkum a vývoj bylinných extraktů jako alternativa k běžným pesticidům. „Už jsme registrovali na celém evropském trhu čtyři přípravky, což je velký úspěch, protože vývoj trvá dlouhé roky,“ pochvaluje si Rudolfský.
Naopak brzdou je podle něj především špatná osvěta. „Té by mohlo být mnohonásobně více. Ekologické zemědělství část české populace vnímá spíše negativně a biopotraviny jsou málo a špatně prezentovány zákazníkům. Vidíme to například v supermarketech, kde jsou biozelenina a ovoce nevalné kvality a extrémně drahé. To nepřispívá dobré pověsti biopotravin,“ upozorňuje Rudolfský. A srovnává situaci se sousedním Německem, kde je biokvalita naprostým standardem. „Budeme doufat, že se to změní i u nás,“ přeje si Rudolfský.
Lepší půda, voda i pestrost krajiny
Že má ekologické hospodaření na vinicích příznivý vliv na krajinu, potvrzuje i Agentura ochrany přírody a krajiny (AOPK). „Pěstování biovín přináší celou řadu benefitů. Jde zejména o omezení chemických přípravků při ošetřování vinic, i když některé se stále mohou v menší míře používat. To pozitivně ovlivňuje stav a složení půdy, povrchové i podzemí vody,“ říká Lucie Záhorová, mluvčí AOPK. Prospěšné je také zatravňování minimálně každého druhého meziřadí, protože přispívá k zadržování vody a zlepšuje zasakovací kapacitu srážek.
V ekologickém zemědělství se také počítá s většími neprodukčními plochami, tedy s remízky a mezemi, solitérními stromy, polními cestami a podobně. „Ekologické zemědělství, a tedy i pěstování biovín, přispívá k větší pestrosti krajiny i biodiverzitě území. V různorodém prostředí se daří více druhům rostlin a živočichů s odlišnými nároky. Přirozeně tam žije více hmyzu, a tím pádem i hmyzožravých ptáků. V neposlední řadě je taková krajina na pohled malebnější,“ shrnuje Záhorová.
Stříkat ano, ale jen přírodními látkami
V čem se tedy pěstování a výroba biovína konkrétně liší od toho konvenčního? Nejznámějším rozdílem je, že ekovinař nepoužívá syntetické pesticidy pro hubení škůdců. Ale jak Kateřina Urbánková připomíná, to je jen špička ledovce. „Důležitý je zejména uzavřený koloběh živin na farmě. Navíc ekologické vinařství má mnohem širší pravidla, která se týkají jak pěstování hroznů, tak samotné výroby vína ve sklepě,“ vysvětluje Urbánková.
A ekologicky pěstované a vyráběné víno se pozná i podle chuti. Nižší intenzita hnojení a menší výnosy mohou vést k větší koncentraci látek v hroznech a výraznějšímu projevu terroir, tedy jedinečného otisku konkrétního místa, podnebí a lidské práce v chuti vína.

title: US-Medienhäuser – Richter pfeift Trump zurück – Ausschluss von Medien aufgehoben
content:
- Präsident Donald Trump muss Journalistinnen und Journalisten von CNN, MS NOW und Politico wieder Zugang zum Weissen Haus gewähren.
- Richter Timothy Kelly hat kritisiert, dass die US-Regierung den Entzug der Presseausweise ohne ein rechtlich angemessenes Verfahren durchgesetzt hat.
- Die Medien sehen in Trumps Verbot eine gezielte Zensur und einen klaren verstoss gegen die verfassungsrechtlich geschützte Pressefreiheit.
In der eskalierenden Auseinandersetzung zwischen Donald Trump und ihm unliebsamen Medien hat Bundesrichter Timothy Kelly die Reissleine gezogen: Er stoppte die Massnahme des US-Präsidenten vorübergehend und ordnete an, dass CNN, MS NOW und «Politico» sofort wieder Zutritt zum Gelände des Weissen Hauses erhalten müssen.
Trump hatte den Ausschluss zuvor mit der Begründung verkündet, negative Berichterstattung sei gefährlich für das Land. Die betroffenen Medien haben sich vor Gericht gewehrt und bezeichneten das Verbot als gezielte Zensur sowie als «eklatanten Verstoss» gegen den Ersten Verfassungszusatz, der die Pressefreiheit schützt.
Richter Kelly ist dieser Argumentation in seiner Verfügung gefolgt. Er betonte, dass die Medienunternehmen ohne die einstweilige Verfügung irreparablen Schaden erleiden würden und gute Chancen hätten, im Hauptverfahren recht zu bekommen.
Bereits in einer Eilverhandlung am Mittwoch hatte der Richter Zweifel geäussert, ob die US-Regierung überhaupt ihre rechtlichen Pflichten erfüllt und den Journalisten vor dem Ausschluss ein faires Verfahren gewährt habe.
Kritiker werten Trumps Vorgehen als Angriff auf die Pressefreiheit und offensichtlichen Versuch, kritisch berichtende Medien einzuschüchtern. Nachdem Journalisten der Zugang versperrt wurde, drohte Trump zudem damit, das Verbot auf andere Medien auszuweiten.
Solidarität der Medien – auch von Fox News
Andere Medien solidarisierten sich rasch mit den geschassten Journalisten. Die engmaschige TV-Begleitung auf Terminen und Reisen Trumps, die über ein Rotationsprinzip grosser Fernsehsender geregelt ist, wurde von diesen als Protestaktion gestoppt.
In einer gemeinsamen Stellungnahme der TV-Sender hiess es, die Öffentlichkeit habe ein grundlegendes Interesse daran, unabhängige Informationen über ihre Regierung zu erhalten. Keine Regierung solle eine Nachrichtenorganisation einschränken, nur weil sie deren Berichterstattung missbillige. Bemerkenswert ist, dass diese Erklärung von allen fünf TV-Sendern im Pool getragen wurde – und damit auch von Fox News, Trumps eigentlichem Lieblingssender.
Pressefreiheit in der Verfassung verankert
Auch andere Nachrichtenorganisationen wie die «New York Times», die «Washington Post» oder die Agentur Associated Press haben sich öffentlich gegen das Verbot gestellt. Vor dem Stand der Associated Press auf dem Gelände des Weissen Hauses wurde als Zeichen des Protests ein Solidaritätsplakat aufgehängt.
Trump geht in seiner zweiten Amtszeit mit zunehmender Härte gegen missliebige Medien vor. Journalisten beleidigt er häufig, wenn ihm Fragen nicht gefallen, während wohlwollende Berichterstattung ausdrücklich gelobt wird. Doch wie in Deutschland ist auch in den USA die Pressefreiheit verfassungsrechtlich fest verankert – eine Hürde, an der die Regierung im aktuellen Fall vorerst gescheitert ist.

title: Indonesia, France partner to elevate aviation safety oversight
content:
Director General of Civil Aviation Lukman F. Laisa stated that cooperation between Indonesia and France has been active since 2019 under a Technical Cooperation Agreement (TCA) covering inspector competency, standardization, and quality management.
"Entering 2026, this cooperation moves into a new phase focused on building a sustainable oversight system," Lukman said in a statement, Saturday.
The Directorate General hosted the 11th Steering Committee Meeting for Civil Aviation Technical Cooperation alongside the DGAC in Jakarta on Wednesday, Sept. 16.
The session was attended by representatives from the DGAC, technical experts, and Airbus, led by Senior Vice President of Airbus Aviation Safety Yannick Malinge.
Lukman expressed gratitude for the ongoing commitment from DGAC and Airbus.
Key technical areas under the partnership include specific approvals for low-visibility operations, Safety Management System (SMS) assessments, risk management, personnel licensing procedures, and the refinement of Indonesia's State Safety Programme.
"Through this cooperation, we hope both civil aviation authorities can continue sharing knowledge and expertise, making our safety oversight capacity more competent, standardized, risk-based, coordinated, and sustainable," Lukman remarked.
He added that the meeting aimed to align future priorities ahead of the International Civil Aviation Organization Universal Safety Oversight Audit Programme (ICAO USOAP), expected to take place in 2027.
While the upcoming audit is a key milestone, Lukman stressed that maintaining safety oversight remains an ongoing institutional responsibility.
Thibaut Lallemand, Director of Asia-Pacific Cooperation at France's DGAC, commended the constructive progress across all priority areas, noting that the insights gained must be fully embedded to build lasting institutional capacity.

title: Network flexibility facilitates treatment-induced recovery in post-stroke aphasia.
content: Predicting the recovery of post-stroke aphasia, particularly in the chronic phase, poses significant challenges. While many studies have focused on static resting state functional connectivity measures as biomarkers for language recovery, there is a significant lack of studies investigating dynamic functional connectivity, which takes into account second to minute timescale variation in connectivity and has been used extensively in other contexts. This retrospective cohort study investigates the predictive value of dynamic functional connectivity for treatment response in post-stroke aphasia. Two temporal metrics, temporal variability and community stability were explored. Temporal variability quantifies the magnitude of variation in the strength of functional connections over time, while community stability measures the mean length of time over which dynamic functional connectivity remains relatively stable. Additionally, a dynamic functional connectivity states analysis, in which time windows are clustered into states using a k-means clustering algorithm, was used to investigate time-varying network properties of dynamic functional connectivity in relation to treatment response. Baseline MRI data were collected for 30 participants with chronic post-stroke aphasia who received a semantic treatment aimed at improving word-finding. Dynamic functional connectivity was generated using a sliding-window approach and the relationships between treatment-induced improvements in naming accuracy and the respective temporal metrics and network properties were evaluated using linear mixed effects models predicting naming accuracy. Specifically, a significant interaction effect of session (i.e. time) and the respective measure was interpreted as a significant relationship between the measure and treatment response. Both temporal metrics were found to be significantly associated with naming improvements, with both higher temporal variability (i.e. magnitude of fluctuations in dynamic functional connectivity; interaction effect: β = 0.45, P = 3.6e-09, η1 = 0.072) and higher community stability (i.e. moment-to-moment stability of dynamic functional connectivity; interaction effect: β = 0.0046, P = 5.4e-06, η 1 = 0.044) predicting greater treatment gains. These findings suggest that patients who benefit most from treatment have neural dynamics characterized by a large magnitude, but low frequency, of fluctuations in network synchrony. Finally, consistent with previous studies, patients who spent more time in a state characterized by higher modularity showed greater treatment response (interaction effect: β = 7.9e-05, P = 6.2e-04, η 1 = 0.025). Overall, the findings of this study provide evidence for the utility of dynamic functional connectivity in studying post-stroke language recovery as a measure that captures interindividual difference in the capacity for recovery. They create a new direction for post-stroke aphasia research focusing on temporal dynamics and their relationship to long-term functional network plasticity.

title: ‘It’s transformed the village’: the volunteers greening up Britain’s train stations
content:
Every year since 1964, towns across the UK have bloomed with hanging baskets and brightly coloured flowerbeds planted by residents.
They wield their trowels in aid of the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition, a coveted accolade for the 1,600 communities that enter each year.
Now, the charity is launching a new award for railway stations to honour the volunteers who keep platforms planted with cheerful flowers and pretty shrubs.
Five of the best have been shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition, marked for their beauty but also for how well they welcome wildlife and withstand changing climate conditions.
The winner, announced this week, was the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland. The RHS said: “The judges were especially impressed by how active the group was in including different members of the community in the station’s activities, from school children, Brownies to other volunteering and gardening groups”. But all of the railway gardens are impressive.
It has been an extremely hot and dry summer in Alresford, Essex, but the gardeners were prepared. Working hard to cut through asphalt to create flowerbeds, they have planted a “dry garden” inspired by the horticultural pioneer Beth Chatto, who died in 2018. Also from Essex, she managed to grow plants in dry ground that had never been cultivated.
“It’s transformed the centre of the village,” said the lead volunteer, Frank Belgrave. Ten years ago the station was described in the local paper as “rundown”. Now, the planting beds rival any at Chelsea flower show.
Belgrave said residents were very pleased their station had received the spruce-up: “It’s wonderful. People sometimes stop by with plants and compost to help us, and we are very lucky to have some lovely volunteers as the garden requires constant maintenance.
“We used to spend all our time watering. So we decided to seek advice and build a dry garden with drought-resistant plants.”
At a windswept station on the west coast of Scotland, commuters may be surprised to find trees heaving with fruit and a thriving vegetable patch. But Jane Connolly, who heads the Cardross station volunteer group, has found a way to create such bounty.
“Since March 2022, every bit of the station that can be changed, has been changed,” she said. “We do have harsh winters – we don’t take summer bedding plants as we don’t get enough out of them – we choose hardy shrubs. We put up windproofing on the shore side to protect the plants but in general we have had very few failures.”
Connolly and her fellow volunteers filled the station with plants from their own gardens and visit most days to tend to them.
Having a pretty, flower-filled rail station rather than a neglected one makes a huge difference to the village, she said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done. I notice stations now wherever I go, even if it’s a window box. People come to our station just to see our gardens.”
Other shortlisted stations include Maghull in Merseyside, where the ticket office’s window boxes are full of pretty flowers and volunteers have planted a woodland. At Wylde Green in Birmingham, overgrown areas were cleared and replaced with pollinator-friendly plants, creating a “bee corridor”. The volunteers carry out an annual butterfly count and have seen numbers increasing.
Keynsham station in Somerset on a hot day looks especially exotic because volunteers have filled it with a remarkable array of succulents, of all shapes and sizes. Like the Essex gardeners, they have selected plants that will withstand hot summers.
The volunteers at the stations have spoken of how social the job is and many have made friends. It also gives commuters a chance to chat. Belgrave said: “It’s very rewarding. Lots of people come and chat, they talk about plants, it gives them a social thing.”
He hopes to get funding for a community hub and coffee shop. “On the platform there is a very ancient station house, to the back of that there was an area which was neglected and used as a community rubbish dump. We have turned that into a garden. Now, we hope we can open a coffee shop on the site.”
In Cardross, the gardeners have become fast friends. Connolly said: “We garden together and there is always laughing and joking and there is often more joking than working! We go out socialising together now as well. It is a very social thing.”
Wildlife has returned to Alresford station, according to Belgrave. “We have noticed incredible amounts of wildlife, bees particularly. Honeybees, solitary bees, butterflies. That has changed a lot, we have seen the return of hedgehogs, we have slowworms.”
The gardeners hope their example will encourage others to get involved.
Belgrave said: “There are lots of stations which aren’t in the scheme, so if people do get involved it would be really good. It would be nice to see more stations planted up.”

title: 'Subsidie voor elektrische occasion vooral interessant voor middeninkomens'
content: Het kabinet wil mensen met lagere inkomens tegemoetkomen bij de aanschaf van een tweedehands elektrische auto. Wanneer mensen overstappen naar zo'n occasion kunnen ze tot 6000 euro aan subsidie krijgen, zo werd gisteren bekend. "We weten dat particulieren minder vaak elektrisch rijden en dit is een manier om ze mee te krijgen", ziet Rico Luman, sectoreconoom Transport en Logistiek bij ING. Volgens hem verdwijnen veel zakelijke elektrische auto's na een aantal jaar naar het buitenland, omdat er te weinig particulieren zijn die ze aanschaffen. "Met die subsidie kun je dat tegengaan." Zo'n auto is voor de lagere inkomensgroepen op dit moment namelijk vaak te duur. Met de regeling wil het kabinet die inkomens compenseren voor de hogere energie- en brandstofprijzen. "Het kabinet vindt het van groot belang dat ook mensen met een smalle beurs de overstap kunnen maken naar een elektrische auto en kunnen profiteren van de voordelen hiervan", liet staatssecretaris Bertram van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat weten. Voor de regeling is in totaal 52,4 miljoen euro gereserveerd. Iemand met een inkomen van 12.500 tot en met 27.533 euro kan 6000 euro subsidie krijgen, iemand met een inkomen tussen de 27.534 en 35.793 euro kan 4000 euro subsidie krijgen. In ruil voor de steun moeten aanvragers van de subsidie hun benzine- of dieselauto wel naar de sloop brengen. Nieuw vs. tweedehands Het aanbod van nieuwe zakelijke elektrische auto's steeg de afgelopen jaren flink. Dat komt doordat leasemaatschappijen ze in toenemende mate op de markt brengen. Maar nieuwe elektrische auto's, met prijzen vanaf 20.000 euro, zijn voor veel mensen buiten bereik. Tweedehands auto's zijn dan een uitkomst. In principe zijn die in trek, constateerde branchevereniging Bovag eerder dit jaar. Er zijn meer mensen die elektrisch willen rijden nu de brandstofprijzen zo hoog liggen. Toch hikken veel mensen ook tegen de prijs van tweedehands elektrische auto's aan. Je kunt er vanaf 5000 euro een kopen, terwijl een gemiddelde benzineauto rond de 2500 euro kost. Bovendien hebben deze elektrische modellen een korte actieradius: ze kunnen niet heel ver rijden op een volle accu. Met name voor middeninkomens Een subsidie kan dan helpen, maar volgens econoom Luman zijn het niet de lagere inkomens maar de middeninkomens die er baat bij hebben. "Middeninkomens kopen bijna alleen maar occasions. Je ziet dat lagere inkomens vaker met het ov reizen en hiermee nog niet over het geld beschikken om die auto te kopen." Bovendien zijn er vaak nog andere belemmeringen die het kopen van een auto in de weg zitten, ziet Luman. "Mensen zullen nog steeds kijken naar de autobelastingen en ook thuisladen kan niet iedereen", zegt hij. Om de subsidie te laten slagen hoopt Luman dat er meer goedkopere elektrische tweedehands modellen op de markt komen. Hoe meer nieuwe elektrische auto's er komen, hoe meer er op den duur ook op de tweedehandsmarkt belanden. Staatssecretaris Bertram werkt de verdere voorwaarden op dit moment uit en adviseert mensen die gebruik willen maken van de subsidie de definitieve voorwaarden af te wachten.

title: Locals, activists welcome State’s move to declare Kunnangudipatti megalithic site as protected monument
content:
Local residents and heritage activists have welcomed the Tamil Nadu government’s decision to officially declare the ancient Megalithic burial sites at Kunnangudipatti near Karungalakudi in Melur taluk of the district as a protected archaeological site.
Locally referred to as “Kurangupadai,” the sprawling 10-acre historical location features a diverse collection of centuries-old Megalithic monuments, including stone circles, stone heaps, dolmens, and menhirs.
The push for official recognition began following detailed local studies conducted by the Madurai Nature and Cultural Trust.
Following continuous appeals from activists and heritage enthusiasts, a team headed by Madurai District Archaeological Officer Ananthi conducted a comprehensive field study and submitted a formal report to the State.
Acting on these findings, the Department of Tourism, Culture, and Religious Endowments issued the order granting the protected status.
Despite welcoming the decision, locals pointed out that the site currently remains entirely open and unprotected, with previous incidents already seeing stones from the ancient structures removed for private construction and domestic use.
Selvaraj, coordinator of the Tungsten Project Opposition and Natural Resource Protection Movement, has urged the State government to take immediate steps to safeguard the remaining monuments by constructing perimeter fencing, installing informational signboards, and establishing continuous monitoring mechanisms.
Additionally, activists have called for systematic archaeological surveys and protection for other neglected regional landmarks, such as the Jain beds, Kallangadu archaeological remains, Aruvimalai inscriptions, and historical sites in Tharkakudi, Sokkalingapuram, Thiruchunai, Kambur, and Kottaimalai.
Heritage experts hope the government will also introduce awareness centres and integrated tourism facilities to help the younger generation engage with the region’s rich history.

title: MML culmina intervención en río Lurín tras retirar 9000 m³ de maleza y material rocoso
content:
La Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima (MML) culminó los trabajos de reducción del riesgo de desastres en el río Lurín, donde retiró 9000 metros cúbicos de maleza y material rocoso acumulados en el cauce, a la altura del puente Pachacámac, informó la entidad edilicia.


La intervención comprendió aproximadamente 300 metros, distribuidos en 150 metros aguas arriba y 150 metros aguas abajo del puente, en un sector próximo a la carretera Panamericana Sur y a la desembocadura del río.
Con maquinaria propia y operadores de la Gerencia de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres, se realizaron labores de limpieza, descolmatación y encauzamiento, además de la conformación de un dique seco. Estas acciones permiten mantener despejado el cauce y facilitar el libre flujo del agua ante un eventual incremento del caudal.
Los trabajos contribuyen a reducir el riesgo de afectaciones en el puente Pachacámac, la infraestructura vial y las zonas cercanas.
Intervención continúa en el río Chillón
Como parte de las acciones preventivas en las principales cuencas de Lima Metropolitana, la Municipalidad de Lima continúa trabajando en el río Chillón, donde interviene un tramo de aproximadamente 4 kilómetros, desde aguas abajo del puente Trapiche hasta el puente Huatocay.
Para estas labores se han desplegado 12 maquinarias que ejecutan trabajos de limpieza, descolmatación, encauzamiento y conformación de diques.
Las acciones buscan retirar los sedimentos, maleza y otros elementos acumulados que puedan obstaculizar el paso del agua y generar puntos vulnerables ante el incremento del caudal.
La Municipalidad de Lima señaló que mantiene maquinaria y personal desplegados en las principales cuencas de la capital para ejecutar acciones preventivas que permitan reducir riesgos y proteger a la población y la infraestructura frente a posibles emergencias.

title: Advancing energy efficiency: innovative technologies and strategic measures for achieving net zero emissions
content: To evaluate the essential role of energy efficiency in achieving net-zero emissions and combating climate change, this comprehensive review was conducted based on a thorough analysis of academic literature, diverse case studies, and industry reports, focusing on key energy efficiency sectors and technological advancements. It begins by outlining global efforts, including the Paris Agreement and the Sustainable Development Goals, which have driven initiatives to enhance energy efficiency across various sectors. The review examines key technological innovations, such as advanced manufacturing, energy-efficient building designs, transportation electrification, and smart grid integration contributing to energy savings and decarbonization. It also discusses policy frameworks, regulatory incentives, and financial mechanisms that encourage energy efficiency. The study provides the detailed outcomes of the different strategies and initiatives, showcasing successful case studies from different regions in transportation, urban planning, power generation, and industry. It illustrates how countries have effectively implemented energy efficiency measures to reduce emissions and meet climate goals. Additionally, the review explores the potential of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data, and blockchain, to optimize energy management, enhance grid flexibility, and promote further efficiencies. Despite these advancements, the review identifies several key barriers - financial, technological, and behavioral challenges that impede the widespread adoption of energy-efficient practices. Finally, it offers strategies to overcome these obstacles, emphasizing the need for tailored policies, innovative business models, and greater consumer engagement. This review underscores the importance of energy efficiency in achieving a sustainable, net-zero future by synthesizing successful case studies and highlighting emerging solutions.

title: Study examines how climate change affects Minnesota's trees
content:
Study examines how climate change affects Minnesota's trees
As our climate continues to change, scientists in St. Paul, Minnesota, are taking a closer look at how it's impacting our trees.
The trees here at Crosby Farm Regional Park along the Mississippi River are doing more than just swaying in the breeze. They're helping scientists better undestand climate change.
"If we think about floodplains, they're really stressful environments," said Scientific Site Lead Marcella Windmuller-Campione. "Everything that lives there has to both be able to survive like flooding conditions ... and maybe also surviving under drought conditions in the same year."
Marcella and the massive number of research and volunteer teams involved planted more than 1,200 trees covering 14 different species across the park.
The goal is to see which ones can adapt to our changing climate.
"Some of those species are a little bit newer to our ecosystem, but we're helping move them to our ecosystem given the predictions of where we're seeing. And so some of our newer species are tulip poplar, northern pine oak, pecan, American sycamore," said Windmuller-Campione.
It's a part of a larger project at 14 various sites across the country and Canada. But Crosby is the first and only one in a city.
Six years into the 20-year study, and Windmuller-Campione says a majority of the trees aren't just surviving, they're thriving.
"We're getting birds living in the trees. We're seeing understory species come in. And the amount that this is doing for our city in terms of stormwater management, providing recreational space, creating cool environments. It's huge," she said.
The researchers say they inspect the tree's every year. They're hoping to get more winter data before making recommendations to forest managers. Right now, the early data is promising as it appears trees are adapting to survive.

title: Cuba Introduces New Hiring and Payment Regulations for Artists
content:
The Cuban Ministry of Culture announced on Friday the implementation of Resolution 28/2026, a new policy outlining the latest rules regarding the hiring practices and compensation methods for individuals working in the artistic sector across the nation.
This regulation, published in the Ordinary Gazette No. 78 of 2026, from pages 157 to 163, supersedes Resolution 44 from June 16, 2014, which had governed the employment relationships within the artistic community for over ten years.
The directive follows the enactment of Law 189 "Labor Code," approved by the National Assembly of People's Power on July 30, 2026. The Final Second Provision of this law specifically tasks the Minister of Culture with setting contractual and remuneration standards for the sector.
The scope of the resolution includes artists and artistic units within music, performing arts, and audiovisual fields, as well as agencies and centers under the Cuban Institutes of Music, Arts and Cinematographic Industry, National Council of Performing Arts, EGREM, ARTEX S.A., and provincial music and performing arts centers and councils, among other authorized entities.
Artistic Evaluation: A Core Requirement
A pivotal aspect of the regulation is the requirement for an artistic evaluation as a prerequisite for formalizing any contract within the sector. "Artistic evaluation is an essential requirement for hiring workers in the artistic field, except in the cases of exemption provided in this Regulation," states Article 3.1.
Exemptions apply to graduates from the professional artistic education system assigned through the Distribution Plan, demobilized military personnel who were previously contracted artists, artists relocated for justified reasons with union agreement, and temporary hires for urgent needs not exceeding three months.
Contractual Arrangements and Payment Structures
The resolution also prohibits employers from hiring artists deemed "devalued." It acknowledges three types of contracts: fixed-term—the primary mode, with a maximum term of one year, which is renewable—, for the execution of a specific performance or work, and indefinite-term contracts.
Each contract must specify, beyond the general elements outlined in the Labor Code, the artistic specialty, the mode of work—individual, collective, or both—, venues of activity, payment amounts and frequency, and personal appearance requirements where applicable.
Regarding compensation, Article 5 outlines three possible approaches: time-based payment, equivalent to a monthly salary according to the level of artistic evaluation; results-based payment, aligned with approved amounts; and payment for the commercialization of artistic performances, which are considered personal income.
The regulation also details that a contract may be terminated due to general reasons or specific sector-related issues, such as demonstrated incapacity or the dissolution of an artistic group.
Additional Regulatory Framework
Resolution 28/2026 is part of a broader set of norms published in the same Gazette No. 78, which includes Resolution 29/2026 on the evaluation of artistic workers and Resolution 30/2026 concerning the contracting and commercialization of artistic performances both in Cuba and internationally.
The new Cuban Labor Code will take effect 90 days after its publication, making its application active by mid-December 2026.
Understanding Cuba's New Artistic Regulations
What is Resolution 28/2026?
Resolution 28/2026 is a regulation introduced by the Cuban Ministry of Culture that establishes new rules for hiring and paying artists in the country.
Who does the new regulation affect?
The regulation affects artists and artistic units in music, performing arts, and audiovisual fields, including various agencies and centers under the Cuban Institutes of Music, Arts and Cinematographic Industry, and other authorized entities.
What are the key contract types under the new resolution?
The resolution recognizes three contract types: fixed-term, specific performance or work execution, and indefinite-term contracts.

title: Total flavonoids of Desmodium styracifolium attenuate nephrolithiasis via reducing calcium oxalate crystallization and renal inflammation
content: IntroductionDesmodium styracifolium, known as Guangjinqiancao in Chinese, is a widely used traditional medicinal herb in Southern China for clearing heat and excreting dampness. It has been historically prescribed for the treatment of urological disorders, particularly urolithiasis (Shi Lin). While the clinical efficacy of D. styracifolium is well-documented, the precise mechanisms of its primary active fraction, total flavonoids of D. styracifolium (TFDS), regarding crystallization and inflammation remain to be fully elucidated. This study aims to investigate the therapeutic mechanism of TFDS in alleviating nephrolithiasis by systematically evaluating its effects on calcium oxalate (CaOx) crystallization kinetics, crystal-cell interaction, and renal inflammatory responses.MethodsThe inhibitory effects of TFDS on calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM) crystallization were quantified in vitro, assessing crystal nucleation and growth. Flow cytometry and microscopy were utilized to evaluate the effect of TFDS on crystal adhesion and endocytosis in renal tubular epithelial cells. RT-qPCR was used to assess the expression of inflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, an ethylene glycol and ammonium chloride-induced rat model of nephrolithiasis was employed to evaluate the anti-lithogenic effect of TFDS in vivo, utilizing ultrasonography, serum/urine biochemistry, and histopathological analysis.ResultsIn vitro assays demonstrated that TFDS significantly inhibits COM crystal formation and growth in a dose-dependent manner. Notably, TFDS promoted the dissolution of pre-formed crystals and effectively blocked the adhesion and internalization of crystals by renal cells. Moreover, TFDS treatment suppressed the crystal-induced upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α). In vivo experiments demonstrated that the administration of TFDS significantly attenuated renal crystal retention, reduced tissue damage, and improved renal function.ConclusionTFDS exerts a potent anti-lithogenic effect by targeting multiple stages of the crystallization process—inhibiting crystal nucleation and growth, promoting dissolution, and preventing cellular adhesion and endocytosis,and suppressing associated inflammation. These findings provide a scientific cognition for the traditional use of D. styracifolium and elucidate the mechanism of action for TFDS-based therapies in managing nephrolithiasis.

title: Photographer wins prize with hen harrier snaps
content:
Photographer wins prize with hen harrier snaps
- Published
Warning this story contains some graphic images
A photographer has won a prestigious award for his six pictures of hen harriers.
Conrad Dickinson, from Hexham, Northumberland, won the conservation award at the 2026 Bird Photographer of the Year competition.
His images showed the birds thriving in the wild as well as the efforts of the RSPB to save the species by monitoring them and fitting satellite tags.
Dickinson said there was no better place to see hen harriers than in the wilds of Cumbria and Northumberland and he was "delighted" to win the award to shine a spotlight on them.
He said: "I wanted to turn my lens on the plight of one of England's most persecuted birds.
"I've had a love of birds since I was 10 years old and especially raptors, in fact one of the first birds I ever saw was a hen harrier at RSPB Geltsdale."
Dickinson said he was "delighted" to win the award but even happier to see the bird get the "recognition and attention it deserves".
Hen harriers are renowned for having spectacular aerial courtship displays, known as "sky-dancing".
RPSB Geltsdale celebrated 13 chicks being fledged, external from three nests this year, the highest number recorded at the reserve in a single breeding season for at least a century.
The RSPB, which has called for greater protection for the birds, said they continued to be "illegally killed" in connection with land managed for driven grouse shooting.
Head of investigations Mark Thomas said he was delighted Dickinson had chosen to focus on England's most threatened birds of prey.
"His striking images not only celebrate the beauty of hen harriers but expose the very real threat of illegal persecution they continue to face," he said.

title: Ethiopia’s Changing Place in the World’s Imagination
content:
Ethiopia’s Changing Place in the World’s Imagination
Addis Ababa, September 22, 2026 (FMC) – For decades, a narrow set of images came to define Ethiopia for much of the outside world: drought-stricken landscapes, famine, emergency relief, poverty and people waiting for assistance.
Those realities were never the whole country. But they became powerful shorthand for it.
Something more complicated is now emerging.
Across Ethiopia, a different collection of images is increasingly competing for attention: wheat fields stretching across irrigated lowlands, coffee moving into premium global markets, millions of seedlings planted in a single day, digital identities connecting citizens to services, new industrial and logistics infrastructure taking shape, and major energy projects altering the country’s productive capacity.
The change is not cosmetic.
It is being produced by changes in what the country is doing.
A country once associated internationally with wheat shortages is now producing wheat at a scale that has enabled exports. Ethiopia began exporting wheat internationally in 2023 after expanding irrigated production and adopting heat-tolerant varieties, turning a former import challenge into one of the most visible examples of its agricultural transformation.
Coffee offers another image of the changing economy. Ethiopia’s coffee exports generated about 2.65 billion US dollars in 2024/25, while export earnings subsequently reached a new record of three billion dollars, according to government figures.
Then there is the landscape itself.
The Green Legacy movement has transformed environmental restoration into a mass national undertaking.
Ethiopia reported planting more than 805 million seedlings in a single day during the 2026 campaign, while the cumulative number of seedlings planted since the initiative began in 2019 reached tens of billions.
The digital landscape is changing too.
Fayda, Ethiopia’s national digital identification system, has expanded to tens of millions of registrations. Digital payments, telecommunications expansion and artificial-intelligence initiatives are introducing another vocabulary into the country’s international profile—one increasingly associated with technological capacity rather than technological absence.
The physical landscape is changing alongside it.
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam stands as the most prominent example: a nationally financed mega-project that has become central to Ethiopia’s electricity ambitions and its broader development narrative.
Around it sits a growing portfolio of infrastructure, industrial, energy, aviation and logistics projects intended to expand the productive foundations of the economy.
None of this means the older realities have disappeared.
Ethiopia continues to confront poverty, food insecurity, climate shocks, displacement and other serious challenges. Emergency needs remain real, and reducing a complex country to a story of transformation would be as incomplete as reducing it to a story of crisis.
That is precisely why the change in perception matters.
The emerging Ethiopia is not simply the opposite of the Ethiopia once portrayed through emergency imagery. It is a country containing both vulnerability and ambition, hardship and construction, unfinished problems and expanding capacity.
What is changing is the range of images available to describe it.
A wheat harvest can now sit beside a famine photograph.
A digital identity system beside a story of aid dependence.
A restored landscape beside an image of drought.
A major industrial project beside the old picture of an underdeveloped economy.
The newer images do not erase history. They complicate it.
And perhaps that is the most important transformation of all.
Ethiopia is increasingly presenting the world with more than one story to tell about it.
The country’s international image is no longer being written only through what it lacks, but increasingly through what it is producing, building, restoring, exporting and attempting to create.
The old images may remain part of Ethiopia’s history.
But they no longer have to be the only way the world sees the country.

MY NINE-YEAR-OLD’S REQUEST seemed simple enough. “Mum, can I get a music player so I can listen to my own songs?”
For any parent, like me, who has winced at their Spotify Wrapped at the end of each year to find their beloved musical algorithm hijacked by their children’s ‘eclectic’ taste in songs will know an ask like this one is literal music to their ears.
Finally, gone would be the reign of musical terror inflicted on my once carefully curated playlists, that now featured earworms like It’s Raining Tacos, Steve’s Lava Chicken and my own personal nemesis Everything is Awesome.
When I was my son’s age in the mid-90s, I had a Walkman cassette player and a horde of tapes from bands I followed and loved obsessively and could happily listen to whenever I wanted. At home, in the car, out walking. It felt like a big step toward being more independent and a real rite of passage, which allowed me to develop my own musical tastes without intervention from parents.
There was also a grown-up thrill in heading down to Golden Discs or HMV and browsing through the latest releases and seeing if I had enough pocket money for a single or an album. Plus, who could forget the frantic, panicked fun of recording songs off the radio before the ads started?
I was excited that my eldest was now taking more of an interest in music, and that he was ready to discover bands and form his own devotions and interests like I did when I was a kid. But there was one big problem that had sort of flown under the radar until now.
Namely, I’ve had to give my son my smartphone, or he had to use the family tablet to hijack my music streaming service and listen away to his own songs. Gone are the days of using a Walkman or Discman, and unless I dusted off my old iPod or minidisc player from 20 or so years ago, I couldn’t figure out how exactly I was going to grant a seemingly simple request for my child to listen to his own music under his own autonomy, without putting a smartphone or device in his hands?
Not only has the current arrangement been cumbersome for both adult and child, but it’s also not been conducive to him getting to listen to music or discover it on his own terms. Essentially, it’s limited his exposure to songs and artists, because it’s hard to do via a parent and their device. What it means is that for pre-phone children, listening to music by themselves and for themselves has become another request for screen time.
Parents are constantly encouraged to limit children’s screen time or delay the introduction of smartphones for as long as possible. We are repeatedly warned about the dangers of hooking young children and pre-teens into smart devices and screen use too early and the damage it can do. Most of us already feel huge guilt over how much tech is in our young children’s lives. On a basic level, if pre-teens want to have anything like the formative relationship with music, bands, and artists that many of us had as a child, it’s invariably happening via the use of smart devices and screens.
Music is hugely important for us all, but especially for children. Listening to music is associated with mood regulation and stress reduction. For pre-teens and teenagers, music can help with emotional regulation and identity, provide a sense of belonging, and create a private space that feels like their own.
But even away from the academics, discovering bands or artists for yourself is a formative experience. While it’s one we may tend to associate more with teenagers, for this slightly younger age group it feels like they are missing out and now experience music at arm’s length. For them, listening to music is predominantly via a parent’s phone, and many of the songs this age group seems to know are from YouTube/TikTok content creators or Netflix movies.
We know that this age group loves music as much as any other. According to research in the UK, 84% of eight-to-fifteen-year-olds listened to music, spending an average of 8 hours 22 minutes per week doing so. The most common device was a phone (63%), followed by radio (36%) and tablet (29%).
The radio is great, and I’m a huge fan, but particularly for pre-teens, it doesn’t deliver the experience they are after. Smart speakers can be another good option, but not every child has one in their room, and even if they do, it tends to deliver that same passive, algorithm-driven selection of songs, rather than putting their own direction in the driving seat.
I’ve had no choice but to go down the rabbit hole to try and find a solution that works. Many parents suggested getting an old phone, wiping it, and only leaving Spotify or another music streaming app on it. It was the obvious choice, but I couldn’t help feeling as though it was ultimately the counterintuitive one.
It reminded me of when, as children, we ate those white stick-shaped sweets that came in cigarette-style packets, and we all walked around pretending to smoke. Yes, technically, I’d not be putting a fully functioning smartphone in the possession of my nine-year-old, but wasn’t I planting the phone seed far too early?
What I needed was something that’s not quite a smartphone but allows my son the chance to listen to and choose his own music. On my search, I found devices that are not phones but are still techy by nature, with touchscreens and phone-style interfaces. Many others were often clunky to use or were too expensive. Most had limited song choices, or the choices and playlists were still made by or via an adult, removing the whole burgeoning and all-important autonomy piece.
I thought perhaps I could upload some CDs to the laptop and get the songs onto an MP3 player that way, but soon felt a million years old because no laptop in the house has a CD drive anymore. Other devices I found required an internet connection to download the music as MP3s and then upload them onto a player. My eyes glazed over at the truncated process involved, having flashback to the Limewire and Napster days.
The search goes on for now, and while it might feel like all hope is lost, I was encouraged to see that Gen Z are leading the charge back toward physical media and screen-free music. Vinyl is now seeing a record resurgence amongst younger generations. According to a recent survey of vinyl fans, over a quarter (76%) of Gen-Zers buy records at least once a month, with 80% owning a record player. Even more encouraging is that the report indicated that half of the respondents saw vinyl and physical media as a break from digital life.
Let’s hope Gen Alpha can follow their lead and continue the charge. Still, at nine years old, I can’t quite see my son starting his very own vinyl collection as a way to listen to Steve’s Lava Chicken quite yet.
Niamh O’Reilly is a freelance writer and journalist.

title: World Rhino Day: Less than 27,000 of the giant animals remain in the wild
content:
Rhinoceros
As the international community marks World Rhino Day on Tuesday, this year’s theme is “Keep the Five Alive”, highlighting the fragile status of the surviving species in Africa and Asia.
Experts say while there has been some success in protecting the prehistoric-looking giants, fewer than 27,000 remain.
Africa is home to two of the species – white and black rhinos - the latter listed as critically endangered with less than 7,000 in the wild.
A World Wide Fund for Nature South Africa project recently successfully relocated 20 of them to Botswana, doubling the population there.
In recent years, the country has come under poaching pressure, particularly in the Okavango Delta.
Since 2003, the WWF’s Black Rhino Expansion Programme has successfully created 18 new populations across South Africa, Malawi, and now Botswana.
The southern white rhino is listed as near threatened with close to 16,000 remaining, a major success story after dropping to fewer than 100 individuals in the late 19th century.
Only two northern white rhino remain, both female, at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Kenya and are protected around the clock.
Most at threat are the critically endangered Javan and Sumatran rhinos found in Indonesia and Sumatra, while the greater one-horned rhino in Indian and Nepal remains vulnerable.
Rhinos are not just impressive animals to spot on safari. As large herbivores, they play a role in shaping the ecosystems around them.
Their feeding habits open up dense bush and create pathways. This lets sunlight in and helps smaller plants and other animals thrive.
Rhino dung also contributes nutrients to ecosystems and can help disperse seeds.

title: Uganda: Tree Planting Campaign Strengthens Gorilla Conservation Efforts Around Bwindi
content:
Community-based organisations and conservation stakeholders around Bwindi Impenetrable National Parkare stepping up tree-planting initiatives as part of efforts to strengthen forest conservation and protect the habitat of Uganda's endangered mountain gorillas.
The initiatives, being undertaken ahead of World Gorilla Day on September 24, are also targeting young people, with conservationists saying early exposure to environmental protection can help nurture a generation that values indigenous trees, forests and wildlife.
At Ruhija Seed School in the Bwindi area, learners participated in planting indigenous tree species, including Croton, in activities led by Change a Life Bwindi in partnership with the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) and other stakeholders.
Joseph Muhindo, an Assistant Tourism and Hospitality Officer in the Bwindi Impenetrable Conservation Area, said restoring tree cover outside the protected area is important because it complements conservation efforts inside the park.
